summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 10 August 2022 report "I Don't Want to Change Myself" rests on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia conducted between 2018 and 2021 across seven states, together with journalists and lawyers, and is the principal evidence base for the finding that every state and the federal territories maintain Sharia codes criminalising gender nonconformity alongside the federal penal penalty of up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping for oral and anal sex.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise same-sex conduct, and lists active litigation there alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia; its account of the state layer cites the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering "sodomy" and "sexual intercourse against the order of nature".

Reuters reported on 21 August 2023 that fears among LGBT people in Malaysia were growing as Islamist opposition foreclosed reform, a political condition that shapes how existing law is enforced rather than altering the text of it.

Human Rights Watch's 24 September 2014 report "I'm Scared to Be a Woman" records that the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, that a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery, and that a woman was arrested more than 20 times. These are resident-facing barriers, but they also mean a visitor presenting documents with a mismatched gender marker is unlikely to obtain any local correction.
localsOnly:
Sharia cross-dressing, liwat and musahaqah offences apply only to Muslims and are prosecuted by state Islamic religious departments; a Muslim resident faces up to three years, RM5,000 and six strokes, while a non-Muslim resident or visitor is outside that jurisdiction entirely.

The Registration Department's routine rejection of gender-marker changes means identity documents generally retain the marker assigned at birth, and there is no administrative route to align them. Domestic sex-reassignment surgery was foreclosed by the 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa.

Documented state conduct against residents includes the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of a trans woman named Victoria by religious officials, repeated custodial terms of four months to three years served in male wards where sexual violence occurs, and the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are subject to censorship. Seventeen civil servants arrested in the November 2025 sauna raid were suspended from their posts.

There is no anti-discrimination statute and no same-sex marriage, so employment, housing and service refusals on the basis of gender expression have no statutory remedy.
outOfScopeNotes:
The United Nations Development Programme and Asia Pacific Transgender Network joint publication on Malaysia is hosted as an image-based PDF; no extractable text was available from it, so its specific findings are unresolved rather than absent.

The Malaysia4U legal guide is a non-governmental compilation, updated July 2026, and its statements on the rarity of enforcement against consenting adults in private and on tourists rarely being targeted are not corroborated in the inventory by an official enforcement source.

Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 suggestion of revisiting section 377B produced any legislative amendment is not sourced here. The outcome of the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge filed after the June 2014 arrests, expected to be decided on 7 November 2014, is likewise not stated in the inventory.

Police mistreatment and impunity in the 2019 killing cases are documented as allegations in the Human Rights Watch reporting; no prosecution outcome for any of the three killings is available in the inventory.
